extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students (patent litigation practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on statutory and common-law defenses to patent infringement based on lack of novelty, prior description/publication, public use or sale, and the role/effect of disclaimers and acquiescence. Focuses on what proof and procedural steps defendants (and patentees) must take and how courts treat these defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Want of novelty / prior knowledge defence
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant must show the invention had been known, used, or described in a public work anterior to the supposed discovery of the patentee (i.e., that the patentee was not the original and first inventor of the thing patented or of a substantial and material part thereof).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff's right relates back to original discovery and may be proved by parol; the defence must show prior knowledge/use/description of a material and substantial part of the claimed invention. Infringement nevertheless must have occurred after the patent date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity required in notice of special matter (prior-use allegations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When relying on the statutory defence of want of novelty, the defendant must state in his notice of special matter the names and places of residence of those he intends to prove had prior knowledge, and where such knowledge/use occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The provision 'shall state . . . the names and places of residence' must be strictly complied with. The notice should also describe whether the whole or only a part of the invention is attacked and identify what public work(s) allegedly described the invention. There is no fixed time limit for setting up this defence, but particulars are required to avoid surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description must be in a public work (accessibility of printed publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior description only defeats a later patent if it was published in a 'public work' — i.e., printed and published in a manner accessible to the public; private or narrowly circulated printed matter may not suffice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will look at the circumstances of publication to decide accessibility; it may be a jury question. The statute's language distinguishes 'some public work' and 'any printed publication' and the intended construction favors publications accessible to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior printed description must enable practice (enablement as prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior description must be such as to give the public the means of knowledge — i.e., of itself enable the public to practise the invention without further invention; mere suggestion, speculation, or incomplete experimental accounts do not constitute a defeating description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary the prior description show reduction to practice, but it must approach the character of a specification by serving as a direction for making, doing, or practising the thing. Examples (Marquis of Worcester) show that mere hints or speculative accounts will not vitiate later patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of foreign prior knowledge/use limited by printed publication/patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere previous knowledge or use of the invention in a foreign country will not defeat a patent granted here unless the thing had previously been patented or described in a printed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the statutory proviso: foreign prior use without a prior patent or printed publication does not automatically render the U.S. patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing the defence — specify whole vs part and check for disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: When framing a want-of-novelty defence, the defendant must determine whether the whole invention or only a part is open to objection and whether a disclaimer has been filed by the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a disclaimer has been filed in reasonable time and the defence only attacks a part leaving a material and substantial part intact, the defence may not be an answer to the action (but will usually prevent recovery of costs). If the defence goes to the originality of the whole patent (leaving nothing new and substantial), it will be an answer to the action despite any disclaimer. Thus notices should identify the particular parts attacked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer procedure and effect (remedy for over-broad claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee who, through inadvertence/accident/mistake, claimed more than he was the original inventor of may file a disclaimer of such parts; the disclaimer must be in writing, attested by witnesses, recorded in the patent office upon payment, and thereafter considered part of the original specification to the extent stated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a disclaimer before suit may preserve the patent for the parts truly the patentee's and allows recovery of costs in some circumstances. If filed during pendency of suit, it will not afford benefit in that suit. Unreasonable neglect or delay in entering the disclaimer at the patent office can defeat its protective effect and may constitute a good defence to the suit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs consequences tied to disclaimer timing and neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: A plaintiff who fails to sustain his action on the ground that his specification embraced more than his real discovery may still recover costs only if he entered the required disclaimer at the patent office prior to commencing suit and did not unreasonably neglect or delay doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the disclaimer is filed before suit but entry at the patent office was unreasonably neglected or delayed, the defence of want of novelty will be admitted as a bar; unreasonable neglect/delay is a question of law for the court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale with patentee's consent constitutes abandonment/dedication
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention had been in public use, or on sale, with the consent or allowance of the patentee before his application for a patent, this may constitute abandonment or dedication of the invention to the public and defeat a later patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acts showing the inventor made and sold the thing for use by others, allowed others to make it with his knowledge and without objection, or let it get into general use, especially with knowledge and silence, support a finding of abandonment. Whether the acts constitute consent/acquiescence depends on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge, acquiescence, and presumption rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge by the patentee of public use or sale without objection strongly raises a presumption of acquiescence; in some cases such knowledge and acquiescence will be sufficient proof of abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct proof of knowledge is not always required; knowledge may be presumed from circumstances and is often a fact for the jury. Long or very general acquiescence may be conclusive.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed lapse of time required after knowledge and acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Once knowledge of public use and the inventor's acquiescence are established, no specific period of time need be shown for abandonment to be found.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case examples show varying periods (from months to many years) after which courts held abandonment; the key is the character and extent of the acquiescence rather than a set time period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use by inventor does not necessarily constitute public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use by the inventor for the purposes of experiment and completion, without selling it to be used by others, is typically not 'public use' that would bar a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts distinguish uses for experimentation (which do not show dedication) from uses that place the invention beyond the inventor's control or are allowed to others without limitation. The inventor's intention in experimental acts is material in this analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraudulent disclosure — immediate assertion required
rubrics_metrics.description: If the invention becomes known to the public through fraudulent means by others, the inventor should assert his rights immediately; failure to do so and long inaction may amount to acquiescence and defeat his rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court has emphasized vigilance: even where disclosure was fraudulent, the inventor's silence and failure to legalize his right promptly may forfeit the ability to obtain or enforce a patent as against the public and innocent third parties.
